title: GaussianFusion: Unified 3D Gaussian Representation for Multi-Modal Fusion Perception
one_liner: Instead of chopping 3D space into a grid, represent it as smooth clouds of Gaussians so multi-sensor data fuses without losing fine detail.
lead: Self-driving cars see through multiple cameras and sensors at once. Today's systems convert all that data into a flat grid called bird's-eye view, like a top-down checkerboard. This grid approach works but crushes detail because grid cells are large blocks that blur fine features, and it makes sensor data hard to coordinate because features just get mechanically concatenated with no learned interaction. This paper throws out the grid and builds a unified space from 3D Gaussians—smooth bell curves instead of boxes—so multi-sensor features flow together cleanly, keep their fine edges, and solve multiple perception tasks from a single learned representation.

paras: A self-driving car has a camera, radar, and lidar (each sends a different signal). To combine them, today's systems project all the sensor data onto a flat grid from above—a top-down checkerboard of square cells. Each cell holds aggregated features from all sensors.

The grid has two fatal flaws: First, the grid cells are big blocks. When you divide 3D space into a discrete grid, you lose fine detail like thin pole edges and delicate boundaries between objects. Second, when features from different sensors land in the same grid cell, they get mashed together by averaging or concatenation. There's no natural way for a camera detail and a radar measurement to genuinely interact—they just sit side by side.

callout.html: Replace the discrete grid with a continuous field of 3D Gaussians (smooth bell curves in 3D space) so features fuse fluidly, preserve edges, and naturally interact across sensors.

panels.title: 1. Multi-sensor input
panels.caption: Camera sees texture, radar senses speed, lidar maps depth. Three separate streams.

panels.title: 2. Old way: the grid
panels.viz_args: A checkerboard grid squashes 3D into flat cells. Fine details vanish, features mashed.
panels.caption: Grid cells average all sensor data per cell. Edges blur, cross-sensor talk blocked.

panels.title: 3. New way: Gaussians everywhere
panels.caption: 3D Gaussians form continuous bumps. Each sensor learns which Gaussians matter to it.

panels.title: 4. Attention-based fusion
panels.viz_args: Camera -> Gaussian. Radar -> Gaussian. Each sensor asks: which Gaussians matter for me?
panels.caption: Each Gaussian learns which sensor modalities are relevant. Automatic cross-modal interaction.

panels.title: 5. One unified scene
panels.caption: All tasks share the same Gaussian field. Detection, occupancy, tracking—same foundation.

steps.text: Project each sensor's features into 3D. Place Gaussians where features cluster.
For each Gaussian, collect sensor features (lists of numbers) from nearby 3D locations.
Compute attention weights—which sensors matter for this Gaussian? Blend sensor signals.
Modify the Gaussian's center, spread, and feature content based on fused sensor data.

steps.b: Repeat across layers, then task-specific heads
steps.text: Iterate through stacked encoder layers. One unified representation feeds all downstream tasks.

paras: The object is the representation of 3D space itself. Instead of a grid, the paper uses 3D Gaussians—each is a smooth bell curve with a center location, a spread (covariance), and feature weights. When sensor data arrives, the Gaussians' properties shift to absorb and blend the signal.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: cross-modal relevance per Gaussian
hidden.name: Per-Gaussian modality attention weights
paras: The paper measures something invisible: for each Gaussian, which sensors are relevant? This is the cross-modal relevance—a learned score that says whether a camera reading or a radar reading should influence that particular Gaussian. In attention-based fusion, the model learns a separate attention weight for each (Gaussian, modality) pair, allowing some Gaussians to listen mostly to camera and others mostly to radar.

The encoder computes these weights via a cross-attention mechanism: camera features query Gaussian features; the dot product reveals affinity. Radar does the same. The weights automatically drive which sensor features get blended into each Gaussian's representation.

heat.caption: Darker means higher attention. G1 listens to camera; G2 and G3 listen to radar; G4 to camera; G6 to camera. Each Gaussian learns which sensor(s) matter.

reads.html: Imagine a Gaussian hovering over a parked car. The camera sees the bumper clearly. Radar sees the metal body. The Gaussian learns: bumper details come from camera (camera weight high), bulk motion sense from radar (radar weight moderate). Different Gaussians make different trades.

The encoder applies cross-modal attention: query signals from camera and radar features interact with key-value signals from each Gaussian location. The softmax-normalized attention scores (which sum to 1 across modalities) determine each modality's contribution to the updated Gaussian feature representation.

mechanism.h2: Why continuous Gaussians beat discrete grids
paras: A grid quantizes space—each cell either holds a feature or it does not. When a camera edge falls between two grid cells, the detail splits and blurs. Gaussians are continuous; they smoothly overlap and preserve edges. When a camera detail sits at the boundary, it activates multiple nearby Gaussians according to the Gaussian's smooth shape, so the edge remains sharp.

The second gain is cross-modal fusion. In a grid, features from camera and radar in the same cell are concatenated or averaged—a passive, mechanical blend with no way for one sensor to emphasize what matters. In GaussianFusion, each Gaussian learns an attention weight for each sensor. If camera-to-Gaussian attention is high and radar-to-Gaussian attention is low, the Gaussian becomes camera-dominant. This learned weighting allows semantic fusion because the model can suppress unreliable signals and amplify trustworthy ones: a Gaussian at a thin pole learns that camera edges are crisp and radar is scattered noise at that location, so it sets camera weight high and radar low, making the final feature reflect just the camera signal.

The third gain is task reuse. A single Gaussian field can be decoded into object bounding boxes, semantic occupancy grids, or tracking states—all from the same continuous foundation. A grid must be re-projected and re-processed for each task; Gaussians generalize.

stages.s: Camera image, radar point cloud, lidar depth
Project multi-modal features into 3D, initialize Gaussians at clusters
For each Gaussian, compute attention from each modality
Blend modality features weighted by learned attention
Update Gaussian center, covariance, feature content
Unified 3D Gaussian representation (detection, occupancy, tracking heads)

math.h2: How the Gaussian encoder fuses one modality
math.words: For each Gaussian, blend multi-modal features by applying attention softmax over modality-specific queries and keys. The updated feature for Gaussian g is the sum over all modalities m of: (softmax of attention score for m at g) times the value vector from m at g.
math.equation: feat_g_new = sum_m ( softmax( Q_m(g) · K_m(g) / sqrt(d) ) · V_m(g) )
symbols: updated feature vector for Gaussian g
query vector from modality m at Gaussian g
key vector from modality m at Gaussian g
value vector from modality m at Gaussian g
convert raw scores to weights summing to 1

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Gaussian at position (x=10, y=5): receives camera query Q_cam = [0.8, 0.6], radar key K_rad = [0.7, 0.9]
Also compute camera-to-camera attention (within modality): 1.40 / 8 = 0.175, radar-to-radar: 1.30 / 8 = 0.1625

math.note: When one modality has high attention weight, it dominates the Gaussian's updated feature, encoding the learned cross-modal relevance.

charts.title: 3D object detection (nuScenes NDS metric)
charts.note: 2.6 point gain. NDS is a combined score across object categories and distance ranges. Grid-based BEVFusion loses edge detail and multi-sensor interaction; Gaussians preserve both.

charts.title: 3D semantic occupancy (mIoU metric)
charts.note: 1.55 point gain while using only 30% of the Gaussians because attention gates suppress uninformative Gaussians, and running 450% faster because fewer Gaussians mean fewer attention computations and less memory throughput.

items.b: Too many Gaussians means wasted compute.
items.html: If you initialize a Gaussian for every pixel or point, computation explodes. The paper uses careful initialization (forward projection plus clustering) to avoid this, but a naive initialization would be prohibitive.

If the model learns that one modality dominates all Gaussians (e.g., camera always has weight 0.9, radar always 0.1), the method reduces to single-sensor processing and loses fusion benefit. The paper does not report this failure, suggesting that careful initialization and training constraints prevent it.

Lidar and radar are naturally sparse (point clouds). Representing them as dense Gaussians may smooth away the pointiness that helps downstream processing because Gaussians blur sharp transitions. However, the paper shows this still outperforms baselines, meaning that the benefit of learned cross-modal fusion and continuous edge preservation outweighs the cost of lost sparsity structure.
When attention is tuned per Gaussian and Gaussians are initialized from true multi-modal projections, one field genuinely serves detection, occupancy, and tracking, without re-engineering per task.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal multi-modal fusion system on a toy 3D scene: one camera image (top-down view of colored objects), one range sensor (sparse depth readings). Initialize Gaussians by projecting both modalities. Train a simple attention encoder (2–3 layers of cross-attention). Then decode into two tasks: (1) object bounding-box detection, (2) occupancy grid estimation. Show that the single Gaussian field serves both, and that learned attention weights differ per Gaussian (proof that fusion is active, not collapsed).
demo.metric_eq: Detection accuracy = (true positives) / (ground truth boxes); Occupancy IoU = (predicted occupied ∩ true occupied) / (predicted occupied ∪ true occupied); Modality ablation: accuracy when camera-only vs. radar-only vs. fused (fused should beat single-modality).
demo.closing: The demo must show that attention weights are learned and vary across Gaussians (not uniform), proving that the model is actively choosing which sensors to trust for each region of the scene.
